headline: Webshot now speaks MCP for AI agents, enabling direct screenshot rendering
summary: Webshot.site now integrates the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing AI assistants to directly render and analyze web pages without manual URL input. This streamlines how AI agents interact with web content.
details: Webshot.site has officially integrated the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling AI assistants like Claude Desktop and Cursor to directly render and analyze web pages. This new capability eliminates the need for users to manually copy-paste URLs or describe visual content to their AI.

The MCP endpoint is accessible via `https://webshot.site/mcp` and operates using JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP POST. It exposes a single tool that allows agents to request screenshots and receive a public, session-free link to the image, effectively avoiding large base64 data in the model's context window.

Each generated image link is secured by a 128-bit random token, making it unguessable and the sole authorization for access. This new functionality is strictly additive, meaning the existing API for raw image output remains unchanged.

Anonymous usage is limited to 5 credits per 15 minutes per IP, with a default full-page capture consuming 2 credits. Users can optimize usage by setting `full_page=false` to spend 1 credit, or subscribe to API plans starting at $1.99/month for increased capacity.

Captures are performed using a real headless-Chrome render, which typically takes 10-60 seconds to complete. MCP clients are advised to set their timeouts to 90 seconds or more to prevent spurious failures on valid captures.

Webshot also registers this tool through `document.modelContext`, an emerging W3C browser API, for native integration in browsers like Edge 147 and Chrome 149 (behind an origin trial). This allows same-origin calls to use existing sessions and quotas, keeping API keys out of the model's context.

The capture process runs in an isolated sandbox, refusing private, loopback, and cloud-metadata addresses. This design allows users to safely preview potentially suspicious URLs without exposing their own browser to risk. Machine-readable documentation for agents is available at `/llms.txt`.

headline: Anker's SleepLab speaker tracks sleep with radar and binaural beats, no wearable needed
summary: Anker's SleepLab speaker uses 60GHz millimeter-wave radar to track heart rate and breathing without a wearable, customizing binaural beats and lighting for better sleep. The Pro model costs $269.99.
details: Anker's new SleepLab speaker promises to track and enhance sleep without requiring a wearable device. It utilizes 60GHz millimeter-wave radar from your nightstand to monitor micro-movements, heart rate, and breathing. The SleepLab Pro model is priced at $269.99 with radar sensing, while a version without radar costs $169.99.
The speaker operates independently with a single button press, eliminating the need for phone interaction or a paid subscription. Users can also stream audio to the device via Bluetooth if desired.

Over approximately one month, the SleepLab speaker learns individual sleep patterns and determines optimal routines. It then employs acoustic binaural beats and lighting adjustments to gradually deepen relaxation and improve sleep quality. Reservations for the device are currently available for $1.
